# 00 — Orientation

## What & Why
You are about to talk **directly to the OS**. This module kills confusion: what is "systems programming", what toolchain you need, and how this repo works. **No skipping.**

## Prerequisites
None. Terminal + curiosity.

## Outcomes
- Explain **syscall vs library call** with a concrete example (`printf` vs `write`) and show the trace
- Build and run 3 programs: **C**, **C++**, **ASM** hello-world on your machine (`mingw32` 32-bit now, 64-bit after upgrade)
- Verify toolchain: `gcc`, `g++`, `nasm`, `gdb`, `python` and know what each does
- Navigate `CURRICULUM.md`, `docs/WORKFLOW.md`, `docs/HOW_TO_LEARN.md` without help

## Examples
| File | Proves | Build |
|------|--------|-------|
| `examples/00-hello-c.c` | C `printf` (buffered `FILE*`) vs `write` (raw `fd`) | `gcc 00-hello-c.c -o hello_c.exe && ./hello_c.exe` |
| `examples/00-hello-cpp.cpp` | C++ `iostream` still ends at `write` | `g++ 00-hello-cpp.cpp -o hello_cpp.exe && ./hello_cpp.exe` |
| `examples/00-hello-asm-x64.asm` | ASM is what all languages compile to | `nasm -f elf64 ... && ld ...` (Linux) / `nasm -f win32` (your 32-bit) |

## Labs
- `labs/01-toolchain-check.md` — verify `gcc 6.3` (old, works for 00-03, upgrade to UCRT64 for 04+), `nasm 2.16`, `gdb`
- `labs/02-first-syscall.md` — comment out `printf`, keep `_write`/`write`, change `1→2` (stderr), reason about `strace`/`Procmon`

## Real-World
`real-world.md` → why Spotify, browsers, kernels all need system programmers — and how this module maps to them.

## Next
→ `../01-machine-hardware/README.md` (do not jump to 02 without 01)


---

# 00 — Concepts: What Is Systems Programming?

![Syscall Layers](./assets/diagrams/00-syscall-layers.svg)

## Normal vs System

**Normal:** `printf("hello")` — C library + OS do everything. You format, they buffer, they choose when to flush.

**System:** `write(1, "hello\n", 6)` — *you* talk to the kernel. You choose fd `1` (stdout), buffer `hello\n`, length `6`. No hidden buffering, no formatting. You pay in control, you gain in control.

> **System programming = direct OS interface via syscalls.** You get control, speed, and responsibility.

## The Three Layers (see SVG)

```
Your code
  → C library (glibc / msvcrt / musl) — friendly wrappers, buffering, `FILE*`
    → syscall trap (privilege boundary) — `syscall` (x64 Linux), `int 0x80` (x86), `svc #0` (ARM), `ecall` (RISC-V) — number in rax/x8/a7, args in rdi/x0/a0…
      → kernel — owns files, processes, network, memory; does the real work
```

* `printf("hi")` → `fwrite` (user buffer) → `write(1,"hi",2)` syscall → kernel writes to terminal.
* `fopen` gives `FILE*` — buffered, portable, `fgetc`/`fread`. `open` gives `int fd` — raw handle `3,4,5…`, `read(fd,buf,n)` — you buffer, you control exactly.
* `fileno(fp)` bridges them. Numbers are OS+arch specific: `write=1` on x64 Linux, `NtWriteFile` on Windows.

## Why It Matters

* **Tools:** `ls`, `grep`, `git`, `docker` — all syscall-heavy. If you can read `strace`/`Procmon`, you can debug any of them.
* **Performance:** 99% of apps use `FILE*`/`iostream` — fine. The 1% (`databases`, `game engines`, `browsers`) need raw `read`/`mmap`/`io_uring` for huge files, low latency, zero-copy (`sendfile`).
* **Understanding:** Every high-level bug (leak, race, file not found, `EPIPE`) is a syscall + kernel story underneath. If you only know `printf`, you guess. If you know `write`, you *know*.

## Mental Model for This Repo

* `playground/` — try anything, no grading.
* `modules/02-assembly` — truth: `gcc -S -O2 your.c` and read what the CPU actually gets. Godbolt > guessing.
* `modules/03-c/systems-api` — the `sys_*` wrapper layer: one `#ifdef _WIN32` in a header, clean API above. You write `sys_read`, it compiles everywhere.

## Key Test After This Module

Can you explain why `printf` and `write(1, …)` both print, but `strace` only shows `write`? And why changing `1→2` moves output from stdout to stderr (`2>` redirect)? If yes, you're ready for 01.

## Try Now

```bash
gcc modules/00-orientation/examples/00-hello-c.c -o hello_c.exe && ./hello_c.exe
# [LOW ] Hello via _write(fd=1)
# [HIGH] Hello via printf (FILE* stdout, buffered) — order may flip due to buffering — that's the lesson
```

lectures.title: 00.2 — Syscall vs Library: The Boundary You Pay For
lectures.content: # Lecture 00.2 — Syscall vs Library: The Boundary You Pay For > **Lecture note — 30 min, interactive, with strace.** Not a README dump — a story. ## Objectives - Tell `FILE*` vs `fd` in one sentence, with code - Draw the three layers from memory and name the trap per arch - Show via `strace` that `printf` ends as `write` ## The Picture *This is the boundary. Everything above is convenience, everything below is the kernel. The trap is where privilege flips.* ## Story — Kitchen vs Waiter **Library (waiter):** You say `printf("hello %d", 42)`. The waiter (C library) formats `"hello 42\n"` into a buffer, decides when to flush, handles `errno`, retries on `EINTR`. You don't think. **Syscall (kitchen):** You say `write(1, "hello 42\n", 9)`. You are in the kitchen. You choose fd `1`, buffer, length. No formatting, no buffering, no retry — you handle `9` vs `-1` and `errno` yourself. ```c // HIGH — buffered, portable, formatted printf("hello %d\n", 42); // → fwrite → write // LOW — raw, unbuffered, exact write(1, "hello 42\n", 9); // 9 bytes, no format, no buffer ``` Why two paths? **Control vs convenience.** 99% of apps want convenience (`FILE*`). Databases, games, browsers want control: huge files, low latency, zero-copy (`sendfile` needs raw fd, not `FILE*`). ## The Trap — Per Arch | Arch | Trap | Sysno reg | Args | Ret | |------|------|-----------|------|-----| | x86-64 Linux | `syscall` | `rax` | `rdi rsi rdx r10 r8 r9` | `rax` | | x86 32 | `int 0x80` | `eax` | `ebx ecx edx` | `eax` | | ARM A64 | `svc #0` | `x8` | `x0-x5` | `x0` | | RISC-V | `ecall` | `a7` | `a0-a5` | `a0` | On Windows, no `syscall` for you — `WriteFile` → `NtWriteFile` via `ntdll`. Same idea, different numbers. ## Try — strace Is Truth ```bash # Linux / WSL gcc modules/00-orientation/examples/00-hello-c.c -o hello_c && strace -e write ./hello_c 2>&1 | head # write(1, "[LOW ] Hello via write(fd=1)\n", 27) = 27 # write(1, "[HIGH] Hello via printf...\n", 34) = 34 # Windows — Procmon (Sysinternals) filter WriteFile, or just reason: _write → WriteFile → NtWriteFile ``` Change `1` → `2` in `write(1,…)` → output moves from stdout to stderr. `2>` redirect now captures it. That's fd semantics, not magic. ## Lab (Lecture) 1. Open `00-hello-c.c`, comment `printf`, keep `_write`/`write`, recompile — still prints. Now you believe. 2. Change `1` to `2`, run `./hello_c 2>err.txt; cat err.txt` — see it. 3. (Linux) `strace -c ./hello_c` — count `write` calls: 2 vs `printf`-only 1? Buffering merges. ## Check - [ ] One-sentence `FILE*` vs `fd` - [ ] Draw three layers + name trap per arch from memory - [ ] Saw `write` in `strace`/`Procmon` (or described chain) ## Next → `00.3 Toolchain` — `gcc -E` vs `-S` vs `as` vs `ld`, and why `objdump -d` is your new `printf`. --- *Interactive: hover the SVG boxes above (if interactive version), click for boundary detail. Lecture note style: story, table, try, check.*

# 01 — Machine & Hardware Foundations

## What & Why
Before ASM or C, understand the **machine they run on**. CPU, registers, RAM, cache, buses, endian, binary — this is the physics of systems. Without it, `struct padding` and `cache thrashing` look like magic.

## Prerequisites
00 Orientation — you can build `hello_c.exe`.

## Outcomes
- Draw Von Neumann block diagram from memory (CPU, RAM, I/O, bus)
- Convert binary ↔ hex ↔ dec, explain two's complement and IEEE-754, predict `0.1+0.2 != 0.3`
- Explain register vs cache vs RAM vs disk by **latency and size** (numbers every programmer knows)
- Predict endianness bug and fix with `htonl`; hexdump any file and read it
- Explain why `struct {char; int;}` is **12 bytes, not 5** — padding, alignment, cache line

## Topics
- Bits, bytes, hex, ASCII/UTF-8; gates → ALU → CPU pipeline (fetch/decode/execute)
- Registers, flags, PC, SP; memory hierarchy (see SVG)
- Endianness, alignment, padding; signed vs unsigned, overflow, float

## Examples
| File | Proves | Build |
|------|--------|-------|
| `examples/01-hexdump.c` | bytes on disk vs in memory, embedded `\0` | `gcc 01-hexdump.c -o hex.exe && ./hex.exe` |
| `examples/02-endian.c` | little vs big, `htonl`/`ntohl` | `gcc 02-endian.c -o endian.exe -lws2_32 && ./endian.exe` |
| `examples/03-padding.c` | struct layout via `sizeof`/`offsetof` | `gcc 03-padding.c -o pad.exe && ./pad.exe` |
| `examples/04-cache-stride.c` | stride 1 vs 16 (64B line) | `gcc -O2 04-cache-stride.c -o stride.exe && ./stride.exe` |

## Labs
- `labs/01-hexdump.md` — write `my_hexdump -C` without `xxd`
- `labs/02-struct-padding.md` — add `struct D`, predict `sizeof` before running, reorder to save bytes

## Real-World
Games pad for 64B lines. Network stacks always `htonl`. DBs tune page size (4KiB) and cache-line.

## Next
→ `../02-assembly/README.md`


---

# 01 — Concepts: The Machine Under Your Code

![Memory Hierarchy](./assets/diagrams/01-memory-hierarchy.svg)

## Von Neumann in 30 Seconds

```
 CPU (registers + ALU)  <->  Bus  <->  RAM  <->  Disk/SSD
         ↕                           ↕
      Cache L1/L2/L3           Memory controller
```

* **Registers:** ~16–32 slots inside CPU, 1-cycle access (`rax`, `rbx`, `x0`, `a0`). The fastest storage you have.
* **Cache:** SRAM, **64B lines**, hides RAM latency (L1 ~1ns/4c, L2 ~4ns/12c, L3 ~15ns/40c). Keep it in cache, you win.
* **RAM:** DRAM, ~80ns, 16–64GB, byte-addressable, 4KiB pages, TLB caches translations.
* **Disk/SSD:** 50µs–10ms, 512B–4K pages, via controller → bus.

> **Why cache matters:** Looping with stride 1 (use every byte of a 64B line) vs stride 16 (64B apart, waste 63/64) can be **10×** — same logic, different memory pattern. See `04-cache-stride.c`.

## Numbers Every Systems Programmer Knows (approx)

* L1 hit 1 ns, L2 4 ns, RAM 80 ns, SSD 50 µs, network 0.5–100 ms
* Cache line **64B** — false sharing killer (`alignas(64)`).
* Page **4KiB** — VM unit, TLB entry. Random 4K jumps thrash TLB, sequential wins.
* `mov rax, [mem]` still goes TLB → cache → RAM if miss.

## Bits & Representation

* **Binary/hex:** `0xFF = 255 = 0b11111111` — 1 hex digit = 4 bits. Hex is compact binary.
* **Two's complement:** `int8` range `-128..127`; `0xFF` = `-1`. Unsigned wraps, signed overflow is UB in C.
* **IEEE-754 float:** `float` = 1 sign + 8 exp + 23 mantissa — `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` (binary can't represent `0.1` exactly).

### Endianness

![Endian](./assets/diagrams/01-endian.svg)

* **x86 = little-endian** — least significant byte at low address. `0x01020304` stored as `04 03 02 01` in RAM on your laptop. **Network = big-endian** (`01 02 03 04` on wire).
* Bug: `fwrite(&hostInt,4)` on x86 writes `04 03 02 01`; `fread` on big-endian reads `0x04030201` — wrong. Fix: `fwrite(&htonl(host),4)` and `ntohl` on read. See `02-endian.c`.

## Alignment & Padding

```c
struct S { char a; int b; char c; }; // sizeof(S) == 12, not 6
// a at 0, padding 1-3, b at 4-7, c at 8, padding 9-11 to align to 4
// offsetof(S,a)=0, b=4, c=8 — compiler pads to keep int at 4B boundary
```

* CPU penalizes (or faults on ARM) unaligned `int` at odd addr. Padding trades space for speed.
* Rule: **sort fields descending by size** (`double 8 > int 4 > char 1`) to minimize padding. See `03-padding.c` — `struct A` wastes 6B per instance, `C` wastes 2B.

> **Lab preview:** You'll hexdump RAM, flip endian with `htonl`, and prove padding with `sizeof`/`offsetof` before the web ever shows you the answer.

modules.readme:
# 02 — Assembly: All Flavors

> **The truth layer. Everything above compiles here.** If you can't read it, you can't debug optimized code.

## What & Why
High-level languages hide the machine. Assembly reveals it: registers, stack, syscalls, ABIs. Learn 4 ISAs so you can read any `objdump -d`, debug any crash, and understand how C/Rust/Go actually call each other. This is the **CORE** — do x64 + one RISC properly.

## Prerequisites
01 Hardware — you know cache line 64B, little-endian, padding, and why `mov` goes through TLB.

## Outcomes
- Write, assemble, link, run in **x86** (32-bit, `int 0x80`), **x86-64** (`syscall`), **ARM/A64** (`svc`), **RISC-V** (`ecall`) — no libc for hello
- Read `objdump -d` / Godbolt and map to C: `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp,N`
- Explain stack frame, callee vs caller saved, red zone (SysV 128B), shadow space (Win64 32B), 16B alignment
- Translate a C function to hand ASM for 2 ISAs and back; use inline `asm volatile` safely from C/Rust
- Bench hand `strlen` vs `glibc` vs `-O2` intrinsic — know when hand wins (and when compiler does)

## Submodules

| Path | ISA | Bits | Assembler | Syscall | What you'll build |
|------|-----|------|-----------|---------|-------------------|
| `x86/` | Intel x86 | 32 | NASM `win32`/`elf32` | `int 0x80` | `hello.asm`, `add32.asm` |
| `x86-64/` | Intel/AMD | 64 | NASM `win64`/`elf64` | `syscall` | `hello64.asm`, `add.asm`, `stack-frame.asm` |
| `arm-aarch64/` | ARM | 32/64 | GAS | `svc #0` | `hello_a64.s` |
| `riscv/` | RISC-V | 32/64 | GAS | `ecall` | `hello_rv.s` |
| `inline-asm/` | — | — | GCC/Clang/MSVC/Rust | — | `cpuid.c`, `rdtsc.c` |
| `calling-conventions/` | — | — | Diagrams | — | SysV vs Win64 vs AAPCS64 vs RISC-V |

![Registers](./assets/diagrams/02-registers.svg)

## Examples (each minimal, runnable, header has BUILD)
- `hello.*` — exit via syscall, no libc
- `add.*` — function that adds two ints, observe `rdi/rsi→rax` (SysV) vs `rcx/rdx→rax` (Win64)
- `stack-frame.asm` — `push rbp; sub rsp,16; mov [rbp-8],0x1234` then `objdump -d`
- `inline-asm/cpuid.c` — `cpuid` via `asm("cpuid":...)` vs `<cpuid.h>`

## Labs
- `labs/01-strlen-4isa.md` — `strlen` in 4 ISAs, bench vs C (10M calls)
- `labs/02-calling-conv.md` — 7th arg on stack, clobber `rbx` without save → crash, fix with `push rbx`

## Real-World
`real-world.md` → Crypto (AES-NI/NEON), codecs, kernels (context switch saves callee regs), FFI

## Next
→ `../03-c/README.md` — C is the OS tongue; now you know what it compiles to


---

# 02 — Concepts: The ISA Is the Contract

![Stack Frame](./assets/diagrams/02-stack-frame.svg)

## What an ISA Guarantees

* **Registers:** x86-64 16 GPRs (`rax rbx rcx rdx rsi rdi rbp rsp r8-r15` + `rip` + `rflags`), A64 31 (`x0-x30` + `sp`/`xzr`, `x29=fp`/`x30=lr`), RISC-V 32 (`x0(zero)-x31`, `x1=ra`/`x2=sp`). All are named 1-cycle storage.
* **Instructions:** `mov`, `add`, `cmp`/`jcc`, `call`/`ret`, `push`/`pop`, `syscall`/`svc`/`ecall`. Each is 1–15 bytes the decoder understands.
* **Memory model:** TSO (x86 strong) vs weak (ARM/RISC-V) — matters in `10-concurrency`.
* **Syscall ABI:** trap to kernel: x64 Linux `rax=sysno, rdi rsi rdx r10 r8 r9`, ARM `x8=sysno, x0-x5`, RISC-V `a7=sysno, a0-a5`.

![Calling Conventions](./assets/diagrams/02-calling-conv.svg)

## Stack Frames (the universal truth)

```
high addr
  [ arg n ... ]  ← caller's stack (7th+ arg spills here)
  [ ret addr  ]  ← pushed by `call` (8 bytes)
  [ saved rbp ]  ← push rbp; mov rbp,rsp  (frame pointer)
  [ locals    ]  ← sub rsp, N  (your vars, 16B aligned)
  [ …         ]
low addr → rsp  (stack grows down)
```

* `call foo` pushes return address; `ret` pops it. If you `sub rsp,5` without 16B align, `movaps` in callee faults.
* **Callee-saved:** `rbx rbp r12-r15` (SysV), `x19-x28` (A64), `s0-s11` (RISC-V) — *you* must preserve.
* **Caller-saved:** `rax rcx rdx rsi rdi r8-11` — can clobber, caller saves if needed.
* **Red zone** (SysV leaf only): 128B below `rsp` usable without `sub` — Win64 has **shadow space** 32B above ret for callee to spill `rcx/rdx/r8/r9`.

## Calling Conventions — The Handshake Between Languages

| ABI | int args | float args | return | shadow/red | who cleans |
|-----|----------|------------|--------|------------|------------|
| SysV AMD64 | rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9 | xmm0-7 | rax/xmm0 | red 128B | caller |
| Win64 | rcx rdx r8 r9 | xmm0-3 | rax | shadow 32B | caller (but callee may spill) |
| AAPCS64 | x0-x7 | v0-v7 | x0/v0 | — | caller |
| RISC-V | a0-a7 | fa0-fa7 | a0 | — | caller |

> **7th arg test:** `long foo(a,b,c,d,e,f,g)` — `g` lives at `[rsp+8]` on SysV, `[rsp+40]` on Win64 (shadow+stack). Get it wrong = read garbage. See `labs/02-calling-conv.md` + Godbolt `x64 gcc` vs `x64 msvc`.

![Registers](./assets/diagrams/02-registers.svg)

## Inline ASM (and why you usually shouldn't)

```c
// GCC/Clang: constraints tell compiler what's in/out/clobbered
uint64_t t; unsigned lo, hi;
__asm__ volatile("rdtsc" : "=a"(lo), "=d"(hi)); // rdtsc → edx:eax
t = ((uint64_t)hi<<32)|lo;
```
* `volatile` = don't delete/reorder; `"=a"` = output in `eax`; clobber = what you trash.
* **Prefer intrinsics** (`<immintrin.h>` `__rdtsc()`, `__cpuid()`) — compiler understands them for optimization. Inline ASM is for what intrinsics don't cover (`cpuid` leaf, `rdrand`).

> **Lab rule:** For every C function you write, `gcc -S -O2` it and read the ASM. Godbolt > guessing. Your `03 C` will make sense after this.

examples.build: nasm -f win32 add32.asm -o add32.obj && gcc add_main32.c add32.obj -o add32.exe && ./add32.exe
nasm -f win64 add.asm -o add.obj && gcc add_main.c add.obj -o add_demo.exe && ./add_demo.exe

lectures.title: 02.7 — Stack Frames: The Universal Truth
lectures.content: # Lecture 02.7 — Stack Frames: The Universal Truth > **Lecture note — 50 min, interactive, with objdump.** The one diagram you will draw for every language. ## Objectives - Draw stack frame from memory (high→low, ret addr, saved rbp, locals, 16B align) - Name callee vs caller saved per ABI and fix a `rbx` clobber - Explain red zone (SysV) vs shadow space (Win64) and when each bites ## The Picture — Interactive *Hover each stack box for what `call` pushes. Click for ABI detail. Ctrl+wheel to zoom.* ## Story — What `call` Actually Does ```asm ; caller call foo ; pushes RIP (8B) → rsp-=8, [rsp]=ret addr, jmp foo ; foo prologue push rbp ; save caller's frame mov rbp, rsp ; new frame base sub rsp, 16 ; locals: 2×8B, keep 16B align before next call mov [rbp-8], rdi ; spill arg maybe ; ... body ... add rsp, 16 pop rbp ret ; pops RIP → jmp back ``` *High addr at top, low at bottom, `rsp` grows down.* `rbp` is the bookmark debuggers use for backtrace (`bt` walks `saved rbp` chain). **Alignment:** x64/A64/RISC-V require `rsp % 16 == 0` before `call`. `sub rsp, 8` without care → `movaps` in callee faults (`#GP`). Always `sub` multiples of 16. **Red zone (SysV leaf only):** 128B *below* `rsp` safe without `sub` — leaf function (no `call`) can use `[rsp-8]` directly. Win64 has **shadow space** 32B *above* ret for callee to spill `rcx/rdx/r8/r9` — even if you don't use it, you must reserve. ## Callee vs Caller — Who Saves? | ABI | Callee (must preserve) | Caller (can clobber) | |-----|------------------------|----------------------| | SysV AMD64 | rbx rbp r12-r15 | rax rcx rdx rsi rdi r8-11, xmm0-15 | | Win64 | rbx rbp rsi rdi r12-r15 | rax rcx rdx r8-11 | | AAPCS64 | x19-x28, sp | x0-x18, v0-v31 | | RISC-V | s0-s11 (x8-x9,x18-x27) | t0-t6, a0-a7 | > **Break it:** Write `foo` that `mov rbx, 42` without `push rbx` → caller’s `rbx` corrupted → crash later, not here. Fix with `push rbx`/`pop rbx`. That's callee-saved. ## Try — objdump Is Truth ```bash gcc -O0 -S your.c -o your.s && cat your.s # look for: push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp, N gcc your.c -o your && objdump -d your | less # look for: 55 push rbp; 48 89 e5 mov rbp,rsp; 48 83 ec 10 sub rsp,0x10 # 7th arg spill long foo(long a,b,c,d,e,f,g){return a+b+c+d+e+f+g;} gcc -S -O0 foo.c -o foo.s && grep -A2 "mov.*\[rsp" foo.s # g at [rsp+8] (SysV) — on Win64, [rsp+40] (shadow+stack) ``` ## Lab (Lecture) 1. Write `my_add` in `x64/add.asm` that clobbers `rbx` without save → call from `add_main.c` → wrong result, fix with `push rbx`. 2. Write `foo` with 7 args, `gcc -S -O0`, find `g` spill, change to 5 args → spill vanishes (register). 3. In `stack-frame.asm`, change `sub rsp,16` to `sub rsp,8` → run → may fault on `movaps` if callee uses SSE. ## Check - [ ] Draw frame high→low with 4 boxes from memory - [ ] Name callee vs caller for SysV and Win64 - [ ] Found 7th arg spill in `your.s` ## Next → `02.5 Inline ASM` — constraints tell compiler what's in/out, `volatile` stops delete. --- *Interactive SVG: hover stack boxes, click for ABI, Ctrl+wheel zoom. Lecture note style: story, table, try, check.*

modules.title: C — Systems Lingua Franca
modules.readme:
# 03 — C: The Systems Lingua Franca

> **C *is* the OS tongue.** Kernels, drivers, DBs, embedded — all speak C. Master it and you can read any system.

## What & Why
C gives you manual memory, the preprocessor, UB, and the **POSIX/Win32** boundary (`open`/`ReadFile`, `fork`/`CreateProcess`, `mmap`/`VirtualAlloc`). No GC, no RAII — you manage every byte.

## Prerequisites
01 Hardware + 02 Assembly — you've seen `04 03 02 01` in RAM and `push rbp` in `objdump`.

## Outcomes
- Pointers, arrays, strings, function pointers — no confusion (`a[4]` decays to `int*`)
- `malloc`/`free` without leaks; implement **bump allocator** (`memory/01-bump-alloc.c` 40 lines)
- Explain stack vs heap, `sizeof` vs `strlen`, UB vs ID vs unspecified
- Use POSIX: `open/read/write/close`, `stat`, `fork/exec`, `mmap`, `socket`; Win32: `CreateFile/ReadFile`
- Debug with `gdb`, `valgrind`/`ASan`, `strace`/`Procmon`

## Sections
- `basics/` — pointers, decay, compile steps (`gcc -E/-S`)

# 03 — Concepts: C Is the OS

![Pipeline](./assets/diagrams/03-pipeline.svg)

## Compilation Pipeline — What `gcc` Actually Does

```
hello.c → [cpp] → hello.i  (preprocess: #include, #define)  — gcc -E
        → [cc1] → hello.s  (compile: C → ASM)               — gcc -S -O2  ← READ THIS (see 02)
        → [as]  → hello.o  (assemble: ASM → object)        — as / nasm
        → [ld]  → hello.exe (link: resolve printf from libc)
```

* **Preprocess:** Copy headers, expand macros. `gcc -E hello.c | head` shows 10K lines from `stdio.h`.
* **Compile:** The real work — C to ASM. `gcc -S -O2 hello.c -o hello.s` then `cat hello.s` — that's your 02 knowledge applied.
* **Assemble + Link:** `as` makes `.o` with relocations; `ld` patches them, pulls `libc`, writes ELF/PE.

> **Try:** `gcc -O0` vs `-O2` vs `-Os` on `pointer-decay.c` — `objdump -d` each, see 3× size/speed difference.

## UB vs Implementation-Defined vs Unspecified

* **UB ( nasal demons ):** `int x; printf("%d",x)` (uninitialized), `*p` after `free(p)`, signed overflow `INT_MAX+1`, `a[i]` out of bounds. Compiler may *delete* your check. Use `-Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined`.
* **Implementation-defined:** `sizeof(int)` 4 on x86, `char` signedness — consistent per compiler, portable if you don't assume.
* **Unspecified:** order of `f(a)+f(b)` — compiler chooses.

```c
// UB that looks innocent
char *p = malloc(4); free(p);
printf("%c", p[0]); // use-after-free — ASan will catch, but C won't warn
```

## FILE* vs fd — The Core Idea

| Layer | Handle | Who buffers | Example | When |
|-------|--------|-------------|---------|------|
| HIGH | `FILE*` (C) / `ifstream` (C++) | C library | `fopen` → `fgetc` → `fclose` | 99% apps, portable |
| LOW | `int fd` (3,4,5…) | YOU | `open` → `read(buf,1024)` → `close` | tools, huge files, zero-copy |

* `fileno(fp)` bridges: `int fd = fileno(f);`
* `03-c/systems-api/01-file-io-compare.c` proves they count same bytes: `HIGH` vs `LOW` → `MATCH!` (fixed `O_BINARY` on Windows to avoid `\r\n` translation).
* **Windows trap:** `_open` without `_O_BINARY` translates `\n` ↔ `\r\n` — your `read` count will mismatch `fgetc`. Always `fopen(...,"rb")` and `_open(...,_O_BINARY)`.

## Stack vs Heap — Where Your Bytes Live

* **Stack:** `char buf[1024];` — auto, fixed at compile, 1–8MB limit, 1-cycle access, dies on return. Fast, limited.
* **Heap:** `malloc(1024);` — dynamic, `free` manual, fragmentation, leak if forget, ~80ns + syscall. Flexible, dangerous.
* **BSS/Data:** globals. **Text:** code.

```c
void foo(){ char stack[1<<20]; } // 1MB stack — may overflow (stack overflow)
char *p = malloc(1<<30); // 1GB heap — may fail (NULL), must free
```

> **Check:** `valgrind --leak-check=full ./a.out` or `gcc -fsanitize=address` — your 03 labs must pass.

## Cross-Platform Wrapper — One Ifdef, Clean API

All `#ifdef _WIN32` lives in one header, not scattered:

```c
int sys_read(int fd, void *buf, size_t n){
#ifdef _WIN32 return _read(fd,buf,n);
#else return read(fd,buf,n);
#endif
}
// You write sys_read — compiles on both
```

This is the `cross_platform.h` idea from the old playground — now you own it.

# 04 — C++: Zero-Cost Systems

> **C++ keeps C's control but adds zero-cost abstractions.** RAII, move, templates — same ASM, no leaks.

## What & Why
C++ is C with **RAII** (`ifstream` auto-closes), **move** (no copy), **templates** vs macros, `filesystem`/`thread`/`atomic`/`span` — all zero-cost, all in `std`. Learn when it helps and when it hides the machine (exceptions/RTTI).

## Prerequisites
03 C — pointers + syscalls solid, you've hit a leak and fixed it.

## Outcomes
- RAII: why `ifstream` needs no `close`, why `unique_ptr` beats raw `new`
- Move, Rule of 0/5, `span` vs `pointer+len`, `filesystem` vs `opendir`
- `std::thread`/`mutex`/`atomic`/`filesystem` — same `futex`/`stat` underneath
- Measure: prove RAII/`inline` are zero-cost via `objdump`/`bench`; know costs (exceptions, RTTI, implicit copies)

## Sections
- `basics/` — RAII file, refs vs pointers
- `memory-raii/` — `unique`/`shared`, `pmr`
- `systems/` — `dir-list` via `filesystem`, `thread-race`

## Examples
| File | Proves | Build |
|------|--------|-------|
| `basics/01-raii-file.cpp` | `ofstream` auto-close vs `fopen` leak | `g++ 01-raii-file.cpp -o raii.exe && ./raii.exe` |
| `memory-raii/01-unique-shared.cpp` | ownership, `move`, `use_count` | `g++ -std=c++17 01-unique-shared.cpp -o uniq.exe && ./uniq.exe` |
| `systems/01-dir-list.cpp` | `filesystem` vs `opendir` | `g++ -std=c++17 01-dir-list.cpp -o ls.exe && ./ls.exe .` |

## Labs
- Port `03-c/wc` to C++ with RAII + `filesystem::file_size`
- `ScopeGuard` vs manual `close(fd)` — measure

## Real-World
Chromium, Unreal, LLVM, Bloomberg, HFT — C++ for zero-cost + control.

## Next
→ `../05-rust/README.md` — ownership at compile time


---

# 04 — Concepts: RAII & Zero-Cost

![RAII](./assets/diagrams/04-raii.svg)

## RAII — Resource Is Initialization

* **C:** `FILE *f = fopen(...); if (err) return; fclose(f);` — you close. Early `return`, `goto`, `throw` → leak if you forget one path.
* **C++:** `{ std::ofstream f("out.txt"); f << "hi"; }` — `f`'s destructor closes. Even on `throw`, even on early `return`. No leak, no `fclose` to remember.

> **Proof it's zero-cost:** `g++ -O2 raii.cpp -S` vs hand `fopen`/`fclose` — `objdump -d` shows same `call close` placement, no extra calls. Inlines disappear.

## Move — Don't Copy

```cpp
auto u = std::make_unique<int>(42); // unique: one owner
auto u2 = std::move(u); // transfers, no copy, u is null after
auto s = std::make_shared<int>(99); // shared: refcount
auto s2 = s; // count 2
```

* **Rule of 0/5:** If you manage a resource, define (or delete) all 5: ctor, dtor, copy, move, assign. Or use `unique_ptr`/`shared_ptr` and define none.
* `std::span` vs `pointer+len` — `void foo(int *p, size_t n)` becomes `void foo(span<int> s)` — bounds, no decay (see `03` decay lab).

## What C++ Hides (Costs You Should Know)

* **Exceptions:** `throw` unwinds stack — if you `-fno-exceptions`, smaller/fast. Know when you're paying.
* **RTTI:** `dynamic_cast`/`typeid` — extra data. `-fno-rtti` for embedded.
* **Implicit copies:** `auto x = bigVector;` copies. `auto &x = bigVector;` doesn't. `clang-tidy` catches.

## Zero-Cost Abstractions — Measure

* `inline`, `templates`, `if constexpr`, `string_view` compile to same ASM as hand C — **prove** with `bench/cache.c` and `objdump`.
* `filesystem::file_size(p)` vs `stat` — same syscall, nicer API.
* `thread`/`mutex`/`atomic` vs `pthread` — same `futex` underneath, but `std::jthread` joins on destruction (RAII again).

> **Lab:** Port `03-c/wc` to C++ with `ifstream` + `filesystem::file_size`, throw mid-read, prove file still closed (RAII) vs C leak.

# 05 — Concepts: Ownership Is the OS

![Ownership](./assets/diagrams/05-ownership.svg)

## One Owner, Compile-Time Checked

```rust
let s = String::from("hi");
let t = s; // move — s is invalid now, compiler error if you use s
println!("{}", t);
let r = &t; // borrow — checked, no data race
```

* **Ownership:** every value has one owner; move transfers; `Drop` frees (like RAII but checked).
* **Borrow checker:** `&` shared, `&mut` exclusive — no `use-after-free`, no `data race` at compile. `Send`/`Sync` for threads.
* **Result:** `Option`/`Result` not null, `Arc<Mutex<T>>` safe.

## Unsafe — Explicit Boundary

```rust
unsafe { libc::read(fd, buf as *mut _, len); } // you promise pointer valid
```

* Safe Rust can't do `mmap`, raw `syscall`, `*mut`. `unsafe` is the airlock — audit it, keep it tiny.
* Re-implement `03-c/cp` in safe Rust: `std::fs::copy` vs `libc::open` unsafe — compare `cargo run` vs `strace`.

> **Bench:** `Arc<Mutex>` vs `pthread_mutex` — Rust adds no overhead, but prevents race at compile.

---

# 08 — Concepts: Memory Is Everything

![Paging](./assets/diagrams/08-paging.svg)

## Virtual Memory

* Process sees contiguous `0..2^48` — kernel maps via **page tables** (4 levels on x64) to physical `PFN`. **TLB** caches `VPN→PFN` — miss = 4 memory reads (slow). `huge pages 2M/1G` reduce misses.
* `mmap`, `mprotect`, `getpagesize()` — see `examples/01-mmap.c` (`page 4096` on Win `GetSystemInfo`).

## Allocators

* **Bump:** `ptr+=size` — free = reset only (arena). Fast, no fragmentation.
* **Free-list:** linked list of holes, coalesce on free — fragmentation = holes.
* **Slab/jemalloc:** per-size caches, thread-local — what `malloc` actually is.

## Cache Coherence — MESI

* 64B line states: **M**odified, **E**xclusive, **S**hared, **I**nvalid — core writes → invalidates others → ping-pong if two threads share same line (**false sharing**). Fix: `alignas(64)`.
* NUMA — allocate on node you run on, else cross-node 2× latency.

> **Bench:** `bench/cache.c` stride 1 vs 16; `perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses` for thrashing.

## Containers = Namespaces + Cgroups

# 10 — Concepts: Concurrency

![Concurrency](./assets/diagrams/10-concurrency.svg)

## Atomics & Memory Models

* `std::atomic<int> x; x.fetch_add(1)` — indivisible even under race.
* **x86 TSO** strong (stores ordered), **ARM weak** (can reorder) — `memory_order_acquire/release/seq_cst` matters. `litmus` test fails on ARM but passes on x86.

## Locks

* **Spinlock:** `xchg` loop — burns CPU, good for 1µs hold + pinned cores (HFT).
* **Mutex:** `futex` → kernel sleep if contended. `RWLock` for read-mostly.

## Lock-Free

* **CAS:** `compare_exchange(expected, desired)` loop — ABA problem, fix with hazard pointer/`crossbeam`.
* Not the same as wait-free.

## Async

* **Readiness:** `epoll`/`kqueue`/`IOCP` — tell when ready, you `read`.
* **Completion:** `io_uring` — submit SQ, reap CQ, zero syscalls. `tokio` (Rust) vs goroutines (Go M:N).

> **Bench:** `10-race.c` → `x=149k` not 200k (race) → fix with `atomic` or `mutex` + `ThreadSanitizer`.

# 11 — Concepts: Everything Is a File Descriptor

## I/O Paths

* `read(fd,buf,n)` → copy user→kernel→disk. `mmap` → map pages, `memcpy` no copy. `sendfile(out, in, ...)` → zero-copy file→socket (Kafka). `io_uring` → batched.
* **Buffering:** kernel page cache, `FILE*` buffer, `O_DIRECT` bypass, `fsync`/`fdatasync` for durability.

## Filesystems

* **Inode** (metadata) + **dentry** (name→inode) + **data blocks**. `ext4` journaling, `NTFS` MFT. `stat` → `st_ino`, `st_size`.

## Durability — WAL

* Write-ahead log: append + `fsync` → apply → crash → replay. Without `fsync`, `kill -9` tears write.

> **Lab:** `my_cat` via `read` vs `mmap` vs `sendfile` — bench 1GB; WAL without `fsync` → kill -9 → torn write.
